title: Shashi Kumar Left Wipro to Farm; His Father Stayed Silent for Eight Years
excerpt: The former lead architect returned from a US tech career in 2010 to build Akshayakalpa Organic — surviving nine near-bankruptcies to create a farmer network that now pays about Rs 1 lakh a month per family.
body:
• Shashi Kumar, a former Wipro lead architect who spent 12 years in technology including a stint in the United States, left his job in 2010 to found Akshayakalpa Organic, India's first certified organic dairy enterprise.
  • His father, a farmer in Tiptur, Karnataka who wanted his children out of agriculture, did not speak to him for eight years after the decision.
  • Akshayakalpa came close to bankruptcy nine times and survived on a Rs 40 lakh rescue from Kumar's wife and uncle before growing into a business reported at around Rs 600 crore in annual revenue.
  • For diaspora readers visiting Bengaluru, Chennai or Hyderabad, Akshayakalpa sells organic milk and dairy in all three cities and welcomes consumers to visit its farms — bookings and product details are at akshayakalpa.org.

When Shashi Kumar walked away from a high-paying technology career in 2010 to make farming his profession, his father stopped speaking to him. The silence lasted eight years. Kumar had grown up in a farming family in Tiptur, in Karnataka's Tumakuru district, watching his father work the land — and his father, who had seen the worst side of farming, wanted his children to study, get stable jobs and leave agriculture behind.

Kumar did exactly that, at first. He completed a Bachelor of Engineering at Bangalore University between 1991 and 1995, pursued postgraduate studies at the Illinois Institute of Technology in Chicago, and spent 12 years at Wipro, rising to lead architect. Then, in 2010, he left the technology industry and returned to farming, founding Akshayakalpa Organic with a group of colleagues — 26 of his Wipro co-workers eventually came out with him, according to The Hindu BusinessLine.

A fascination that started in 1991

Kumar's interest in natural farming predated his corporate career. Soon after finishing his degree in 1991, he visited Cherkady Ramachandra Rao, a farmer near Udupi who cultivated several crops sustainably on just two acres. Rao's farm showed him agriculture could deliver both self-sufficiency and economic stability, and Kumar returned over successive years to learn first-hand.

That conviction — that farming should be a desired profession for India's youth — became Akshayakalpa's founding mission. The Tiptur-headquartered company was built around giving farmers regular cash flow, starting with dairy and later expanding into soil management, beekeeping, poultry and bananas.

Nine near-bankruptcies and a family rescue

The early years were punishing. Kumar says Akshayakalpa came close to bankruptcy nine times. At its darkest point, the venture survived on a Rs 30 lakh infusion from his wife, Shilpa G, and a Rs 10 lakh contribution from his uncle, Dr Muni Reddy — Rs 40 lakh that, by Kumar's account, kept the company afloat.

"My father thought farming is risky as he was a farmer and saw the worst side of it."

— Shashi Kumar, co-founder and CEO, Akshayakalpa Organic

Speaking to BusinessLine, Kumar put the family cost plainly: "And for 8-10 years, my father didn't speak to me. There are a lot of issues like that," he said.

What Akshayakalpa looks like now

The model that emerged pays farmers first. Akshayakalpa says the average monthly payout to a farmer is about Rs 1 lakh paid directly, and company figures cited in recent reports put the average payout per farming family at Rs 1.28 lakh in the last financial year. "Our fundamental belief is that if a farmer is not making money, nobody will make money. So you can't make money by short-changing a farmer," Kumar told BusinessLine.

The company now works with roughly 2,800 farmers — about 2,200 of them supplying milk in Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Telangana — and around 1,200 women participate in the network. The average age of its farmers is about 32, well below the ageing profile of Indian agriculture nationally. Its products — milk, curd, cheese, ghee, paneer, vegetables and greens — sell in Bengaluru, Chennai and Hyderabad, and it has begun groundwork in Maval, between Mumbai and Pune, to build a farmer network there, a two-and-a-half to three-year process before any sales begin.

Why young people leave — and what would bring them back

Kumar's diagnosis of rural flight is direct: young people leave because agriculture rarely offers a stable or dignified livelihood. Universities teach crop science, he argues, but real farming demands holistic knowledge of soil, weather, animals and local ecology. His answer is to make farming worth choosing — monthly income, organic certification taking around two-and-a-half to three years per farmer, and practices such as letting cattle roam untethered.

For Indian professionals abroad weighing a return home, Kumar's story is a rare documented case of reverse migration that survived its own early collapse — at the price of nearly a decade of silence from his father. Readers can explore Akshayakalpa's farm visits and products through its official website.
